Exact_English_Answer: Millet should be planted at the beginning of the rainy season when adequate rainfall is expected.
Evidence_Source: Akinseye et al. (2016), Evaluation of the onset and length of growing season to define planting date â€” a case study for Mali (ICRISAT OAR 8695). https://oar.icrisat.org/8695/
Supported_Claims: Millet planting in Mali is linked to the onset of the rainy/growing season and sufficient rainfall/soil moisture conditions.
Qualification: The source supports the underlying claim rather than reproducing the KB sentence verbatim.

Evidence_Source: ICAR-AICRP on Pearl Millet, Technologies. https://aicpmip.res.in/technologies.html
Supported_Claims: Pearl millet sowing depth of approximately 2.5â€“3 cm.
Qualification: The source specifies 2.5â€“3 cm, while the KB answer says 2â€“3 cm; the KB range is therefore slightly broader than the directly stated recommendation. A second ICRISAT Sahel study provides supporting experimental context.

Exact_English_Answer: Tomato plants should be watered regularly, especially during dry periods, while avoiding waterlogging.
Evidence_Source: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension, Commercial Tomato Production Handbook, Bulletin 1312. https://extension.uga.edu/publications/detail.html?number=B1312
Supported_Claims: Tomatoes require adequate irrigation, particularly at critical growth stages and during moisture stress; excessive soil saturation/waterlogging should be avoided.
Qualification: The source is Georgia-specific. It supports the general tomato-irrigation principle, not a Mali-specific irrigation schedule.

Exact_English_Answer: Soil testing and observation of crop symptoms can help identify nutrient deficiencies.
Evidence_Source: FAO, Plant Nutrition for Food Security: A Guide to Integrated Nutrient Management, Chapter 4. https://www.fao.org/4/a0443e/a0443e.pdf
Supported_Claims: Soil testing and observation of characteristic crop symptoms are recognized approaches for identifying or assessing nutrient deficiencies.
Qualification: Visual symptoms can have multiple causes and may require confirmation through soil or plant analysis.

Exact_English_Answer: Farmers can control armyworms through regular monitoring, biological control, and recommended pesticides when necessary.
Evidence_Source: FAO sources on fall armyworm and African armyworm: https://www.fao.org/family-farming/detail/en/c/1755421/ ; https://www.fao.org/family-farming/detail/en/c/1620521/
Supported_Claims: Monitoring, biological control and pesticide use within an integrated-management approach are supported for specific armyworm species.
Qualification: The KB uses the generic term 'armyworms'. Fall armyworm and African armyworm are distinct pests; species identification/clarification is required before validating the generic answer.

Exact_English_Answer: Farmers can use drought-tolerant crops, conserve soil moisture, and diversify their farming activities.
Evidence_Source: FAO, Integrating climate resilience into agricultural production for food security in rural areas of Mali. https://www.fao.org/agriculture/ippm/projects/mali/gcp-mli-033-ldf/en/
Supported_Claims: Drought-tolerant/early-maturing varieties, improved soil and water management including moisture conservation, and diversification are climate-resilience measures relevant to Mali.
Qualification: The evidence is Mali-specific and supports all three components at the level of general adaptation practice.

Exact_English_Answer: Soil erosion can be reduced through contour farming, mulching, cover crops, and tree planting.
Evidence_Source: ICRISAT studies on contour-based soil and water conservation in Southern Mali; FAO conservation-agriculture guidance. https://oar.icrisat.org/11381/ ; https://www.fao.org/conservation-agriculture/in-practice/soil-organic-cover/en/
Supported_Claims: Contour-based practices reduce runoff/soil loss; mulch and vegetative cover protect soil; tree/revegetation measures can help stabilize degraded land.
Qualification: No single cited source independently proves all four practices. Evidence is combined across Mali-specific ICRISAT research and broader FAO guidance.

Exact_English_Answer: Crops are ready for harvest when they reach physiological maturity and show characteristic signs such as color change and drying.
Evidence_Source: FAO, Agricultural engineering in development â€” The harvest. https://www.fao.org/4/t0522e/t0522e05.htm
Supported_Claims: Harvest timing should consider physiological/appropriate maturity and crop-specific physical indicators such as colour, grain characteristics, moisture and drying.
Qualification: Maturity indicators vary by crop and intended use; the source supports a general principle rather than one universal indicator.

Exact_English_Answer: Grains should be dried to a safe moisture content before storage to prevent spoilage.
Evidence_Source: FAO, Agricultural engineering in development â€” Drying and Storage. https://www.fao.org/4/t0522e/T0522E08.htm ; https://www.fao.org/4/t0522e/T0522E09.htm
Supported_Claims: Drying grain to an appropriate safe-moisture level before storage reduces deterioration and losses associated with mould, insects and premature germination.
Qualification: Safe moisture content varies by grain and storage conditions; it is not one universal percentage.

Exact_English_Answer: Certified seeds have high germination rates, are genetically pure, and are less likely to carry diseases.
Evidence_Source: FAO seed-system and seed-quality-control guidance. https://www.fao.org/agriculture/crops/thematic-sitemap/theme/compendium/tools-guidelines/what-are-seed-systems/en/ ; https://www.fao.org/4/y4011e/y4011e0v.htm
Supported_Claims: Certification systems assess germination, varietal identity/purity and seed health and require compliance with applicable standards.
Qualification: Certification does not mean absolute genetic purity, guaranteed germination, or complete freedom from disease; the safer interpretation is compliance with applicable quality standards and reduced risk of seed-borne disease.
